questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical per-tenant traffic routing, feature flag management, and end-to-end validation with minimal manifests in CNF/Kubernetes environments.

## Key Concepts
- Sidecar-based traffic routing with per-tenant control
- Namespace-scoped ConfigMap for cnf.canary.enabled and cnf.canary.sample-rate
- Deterministic hashing for consistent bucket allocation
- Minimal YAML manifests for quick validation

## Code Example

**Namespace-scoped ConfigMap:**
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cnf.canary
  namespace: tenant-a
data:
  cnf.canary.enabled: "true"
  cnf.canary.sample-rate: "5"
```

**Canary Deployment:**
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: canary-resource
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  selector:
    app: resource
    version: canary
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: stable-resource
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  selector:
    app: resource
    version: stable
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
```

**Sidecar Configuration:**
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cnf-gateway
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cnf-gateway
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: gateway
          image: cnf-gateway:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          volumeMounts:
            - name: cnf-config
              mountPath: /config
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: cnf-config
          configMap:
            name: cnf.canary
```

## Validation
Apply the manifests and verify routing:
```bash
kubectl apply -f namespace.yaml
kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml
kubectl apply -f services.yaml
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

# Test canary routing
export TENANT_ID="tenant-a"
for i in {1..100}; do
  curl -H "X-TENANT-ID: $TENANT_ID" http://cnf-gateway.tenant-a.svc/v2/resource
done
```

Expected: ~5% of requests route to canary-resource, 95% to stable-resource based on deterministic tenant ID hashing.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates practical skills in per-tenant policy enforcement, dynamic configuration reload, and how a sidecar can drive access control using Kubernetes-native resources.

## Key Concepts
- Per-tenant ACLs loaded from ConfigMaps with tenant-specific naming conventions
- Dynamic config reload and conflict resolution between cluster-wide and namespace-scoped policies
- Sidecar architecture and policy evaluation pipeline
- Kubernetes ConfigMap watch mechanisms and Informers
- End-to-end testing within a single namespace

## Code Example
```yaml
# Example policy
tenant: tenant-a
rules:
  - path: /api/v1/users/*
    methods: ["GET","POST"]
  - path: /health
    methods: ["GET"]
```

## Implementation Details

### ConfigMap Structure
The sidecar watches ConfigMaps matching the pattern `cnf.acl.{tenant}.yaml` in the tenant's namespace. Namespace-scoped overrides follow the naming convention `cnf.acl.{tenant}.override.yaml`.

### Watch Mechanism
Use a Kubernetes Informer to watch ConfigMap changes. On update, the sidecar re-parses the YAML, merges policies (namespace overrides take precedence), and updates the in-memory rule engine without pod restart.

### Conflict Resolution
When cluster-wide and namespace-scoped policies conflict, apply a merge strategy where namespace-specific rules override cluster defaults for the same path and method combination. Log conflicts for observability.

### Testing Manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: tenant-a-test
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cnf.acl.tenant-a.yaml
  namespace: tenant-a-test
data:
  policy.yaml: |
    tenant: tenant-a
    rules:
      - path: /api/v1/users/*
        methods: ["GET", "POST"]
      - path: /health
        methods: ["GET"]
```
